extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, humor scholars, students and teachers of humor/comedy writing
extracted.subtask_description: Use Arthur Asa Berger's list of 45 humor techniques (grouped into four categories) to analyze or produce humorous texts; includes examples and disciplinary lenses for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce situations or elements that are wildly unreasonable or nonsensical to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used broadly across texts to create incongruity or surprise; can be combined with other techniques. No single explicit example in this article, but included within the 45 building-block techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accidental events or mishaps as the basis for comic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accident can be a plot driver that triggers further techniques (e.g., coincidence → mistake). Often paired with slapstick or grotesque consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer indirectly to well-known texts, figures, or events so the audience's recognition produces amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Benjamin Franklin verse alluding to Samson's jaw—combined with Analogy and Insult. Allusion often relies on shared cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humor by comparing unlike things in a way that highlights comedic similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example with Franklin: Jack’s jaw compared to the jaw of an ass (Biblical Samson) producing comic effect; often pairs with Allusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before/After
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast a prior state with a later one to create surprise or reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for establishing expectations and then subverting them; can work as setup for Reversal or Disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombast
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inflated, grandiose language or exaggerated style to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bombast ridicules pretension or mismatch between style and subject; may be paired with Understatement for contrast (reverse technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodic or exaggerated imitation that treats serious subjects as trivial or trivial subjects as serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works via incongruity of tone; often overlaps with Parody and Caricature in dramatic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerate distinctive features of a person or type to create a comic portrait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to create comic types; relates to Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' and to stereotypes or ridiculing social types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue
rubrics_metrics.description: List items or features in a way that accumulates comic effect (long lists, escalating detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogues can produce humor by accumulation, by escalating absurdity, or by contrast between items; useful for theme & variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chase Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pursuit and frantic motion (literal or narrative) as a source of physical/comic tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in slapstick traditions; pairs with Speed, Slapstick, and Grotesque physicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on unlikely coincidences to create surprising and comic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: minister/priest/rabbi fridge joke begins with coincidence; often used as a setup for Mistakes, Facetiousness, or Reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtapose two things to expose incongruity or similarity that yields humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to Analogy but may be simpler; used to highlight incongruity through juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Play with or subvert formal definitions to create comic reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition jokes exploit literal meanings vs. expected meanings (connects to Over literalness/Literalness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment (Defeated Expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set expectations up and then deny or frustrate them; punch lines often rely on this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central technique for many jokes; example: gay brothers joke uses defeated expectation in the bartender's question and punch line. Berger emphasizes this as key in rhetorical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eccentricity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize people as odd or deviant from norms to create comic types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tanning man who sprinkles sand on himself to tan his penis; can combine with Mistakes and Exposure. Draws on comic types and Bergson's 'mechanical' idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit moments of shame, awkwardness, or social faux pas for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often produces sympathetic laughter; example elements appear in exposure/exhibitionism jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Overstate characteristics, actions, or consequences to absurd proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be reversed as Understatement; often used with Caricature, Bombast, or Grotesque. Berger notes opposites can be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal private, taboo, or hidden information to create shock and laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sexual exposure in the tanning joke; exposure often intersects with Embarrassment and Grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facetiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat serious matters lightly or flippantly, often with intentional levity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rabbi explains smoking in a refrigerator—facetious explanation; can undercut gravity and produce comic relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Use distorted, bizarre, or exaggeratedly ugly imagery or situations for shock-comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pairs with Slapstick or Caricature; useful to produce visceral laughter or discomforted amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit characters' lack of knowledge or misunderstanding as source of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often appears with Mistakes, Misunderstanding, or Over literalness; creates dramatic irony when audience knows more than characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimic someone's speech, behavior, or style to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to Mimicry and Impersonation; effective when target is recognizable and the imitation emphasizes quirks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt another person's persona or voice to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performer-based technique; overlaps with Imitation and Mimicry; useful in live comedy and character-driven sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantilism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use childlike behavior, regression, or naiveté to elicit laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can create contrast with adult contexts or responsibilities; may be sympathetic or derisive depending on framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Attack or belittle someone verbally to generate laughter (repartee, put-downs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often social and can build in-group cohesion; risk of offense. Example: Franklin example includes Insult when comparing characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a gap between expectation and outcome, often through contrast of meaning or intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad category that includes verbal irony, situational irony, and dramatic irony; connects strongly to Reversal and Disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalness (Over literalness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit literal interpretations of figurative language or situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ladder joke — 'drinks on the house' taken literally; pairs with Misunderstanding to produce punch lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy sounds, gestures, or mannerisms to highlight and exaggerate for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close to Imitation/Impersonation; often used in physical comedy and character work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use erroneous beliefs, misperceptions, or actions by characters to generate humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tanning-man misunderstanding; minister/priest/rabbi joke involves mistaken assumptions leading to farce. Mistakes often cascade into further techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters interpret situations or remarks incorrectly, producing comic consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Why did moron bring a ladder?'—Misunderstanding + Over literalness. Misunderstanding is a staple in many jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate the style/form of another work, genre, or person in a way that ridicules or pays homage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often relies on audience familiarity with the target; overlaps with Burlesque and Satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns / Wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit multiple meanings, similar sounds, or linguistic ambiguities for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal technique that can be light or groan-inducing; effective in repartee and defined-joke formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartee
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick, witty exchanges between characters producing rapid-fire humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on timing and sharpness; often scored by speed and social cleverness; pairs well with Sarcasm and Insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat words, phrases, actions, or scenarios to build expectation and then subvert or escalate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: gay brothers joke uses repetition (first, second, third brother) to heighten the punch line; repetition can intensify comic effect when combined with escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Invert expectations or swap roles/elements so that the outcome is opposite the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Radio Erevan jokes where 'yes' is followed by reversed facts; identified as a dominant technique in that joke family. Reversal is a core mechanism of punch lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Make fun of someone or something to diminish or mock, producing laughter often at the target's expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely tied to Superiority theory; can build group cohesion but risks hostility; often paired with Stereotypes or Insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Present characters or situations as inflexible or mechanical to create comic contrast with fluid reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to Bergson's comic types; can be used to expose absurdity in social roles or habits (e.g., all family members sharing the same trait).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cutting, often ironic remarks intended to mock or convey contempt under the guise of praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A form of verbal irony that depends on tone and context; can be biting and alienating if misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Use humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize institutions, politics, or social mores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Radio Erevan jokes satirize politics/socialism. Satire tends toward social critique rather than pure joke mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale / Size
rubrics_metrics.description: Use disparity in size or scale (literal or figurative) to create comic contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be visual (giant vs tiny) or conceptual (big concern over small matter); pairs with Grotesque or Slapstick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical comedy focused on pratfalls, collisions, and exaggerated bodily harm or mishap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used in chase scenes and with Speed; works best visually or in performance contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rapid pacing, quick reactions, or accelerated escalation to heighten comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: repartee and chase scenes rely on speed; timing is crucial—too slow kills the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit generalized, oversimplified traits of groups for immediate recognition and comedic shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: UN/Elephant joke leverages national stereotypes. Effective but ethically risky—can perpetuate prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme & Variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore a central comic idea through repeated variations that escalate or twist the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: lists of national takes on 'The Elephant' (Theme & Variation) or building a gag via successive permutations; pairs well with Repetition and Catalogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmasking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal true motives, identities, or hypocrisies to produce comic surprise or schadenfreude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unmasking often functions as a reveal/punch line; connects to Exposure and Disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify techniques into four categories (Language, Logic, Identity, Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the 45 techniques into four high-level categories: Language, Logic, Identity, and Action (visual humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 1 groups techniques by category to aid analysis and application; use categories to choose complementary techniques and to analyze a text's dominant mode(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use techniques as building blocks; combine and deconstruct
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the 45 techniques as modular elements that can be combined to create complex humor or used to deconstruct existing humorous texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berger presents analyses showing multiple techniques operating simultaneously (e.g., a joke may employ Reversal, Satire, and Repetition). When producing humor, mix techniques to suit personality and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer techniques over rote joke-telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Be funny by applying humor techniques rather than relying solely on telling preformed jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berger gives three reasons: (1) a joke may be lousy; (2) you may not tell it well; (3) the listener may have heard it before. Using techniques lets you create original humor tailored to your persona and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques can be inverted (use opposites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the reverse of a technique (e.g., Understatement vs. Exaggeration) as an equally valid method to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes many techniques have useful opposites; choose inversion deliberately to subvert expectations or create subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple disciplinary lenses when analyzing humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze jokes using different academic perspectives (rhetoric, semiotics, communication theory, psychology, sociology, philosophy, political science, feminism) to reveal different facets of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berger demonstrates the gay-brothers joke analyzed across eight perspectives, showing each lens highlights different functions and criteria (e.g., function for group cohesion in sociology vs. paradigmatic oppositions in semiotics). Use multidisciplinary analysis for fuller understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'why people laugh' from 'what makes them laugh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate theories of why laughter exists (origin) from the practical techniques that produce laughter in texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berger focuses on 'what makes people laugh' (techniques) rather than ontological theories; for production/evaluation, emphasize techniques over speculative why-theories.
